CHAIR ( Senator Darmanin ): I declare open this hearing of the Economics Legislation Committee into the 2026-27 budget estimates. I begin by acknowledging the traditional custodians of the land on which we meet today and pay my respects to their elders past and present, and I extend that respect to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples here today. The committee is due to report to the Senate on Tuesday 23 June 2026. The committee has set 12 June 2026 as the date by which senators are to submit written questions on notice and 24 July 2026 as the date for the return of answers to questions taken on notice. The committee's proceedings today will begin with representatives from the Australian Securities and Investments Commission.

Under standing order 26, the committee must take all evidence in public session. This includes answers to questions on notice. I remind all witnesses that in giving evidence to the committee they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It is unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee, and such action may be treated by the Senate as a contempt. It is also a contempt to give false or misleading evidence.

The Senate has endorsed the following test of relevance of questions at estimates hearings: any questions going to the operations or financial positions of the departments and agencies which are seeking funds in estimates are relevant questions for the purposes of estimates hearings. I remind officers that the Senate has resolved that there are no areas in connection with the expenditure of public funds where any person has a discretion to withhold details or explanations from the parliament or its committees unless the parliament has expressly provided otherwise. The Senate has resolved also that an officer of a department of the Commonwealth shall not be asked to give opinions on matters of policy and shall be given reasonable opportunity to refer questions asked of the officer to superior officers or to a minister. This resolution does not preclude questions asking for explanations of policies or factual questions about when and how policies were adopted.

Witnesses are reminded of the Senate order specifying the process by which a claim of public interest immunity should be raised, and I incorporate the public interest immunity statement into the Hansard.

The extract read as follows—

Public interest immunity claims

That the Senate—

(a) notes that ministers and officers have continued to refuse to provide information to Senate committees without properly raising claims of public interest immunity as required by past resolutions of the Senate;

(b) reaffirms the principles of past resolutions of the Senate by this order, to provide ministers and officers with guidance as to the proper process for raising public interest immunity claims and to consolidate those past resolutions of the Senate;

(c) orders that the following operate as an order of continuing effect:

(1) If:

(a) a Senate committee, or a senator in the course of proceedings of a committee, requests information or a document from a Commonwealth department or agency; and

(b) an officer of the department or agency to whom the request is directed believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the officer shall state to the committee the ground on which the officer believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, and specify the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(2) If, after receiving the officer's statement under paragraph (1), the committee or the senator requests the officer to refer the question of the disclosure of the information or document to a responsible minister, the officer shall refer that question to the minister.

(3) If a minister, on a reference by an officer under paragraph (2), concludes that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the minister shall provide to the committee a statement of the ground for that conclusion, specifying the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(4) A minister, in a statement under paragraph (3), shall indicate whether the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee could result only from the publication of the information or document by the committee, or could result, equally or in part, from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee as in camera evidence.

(5) If, after considering a statement by a minister provided under paragraph (3), the committee concludes that the statement does not sufficiently justify the withholding of the information or document from the committee, the committee shall report the matter to the Senate.

(6) A decision by a committee not to report a matter to the Senate under paragraph (5) does not prevent a senator from raising the matter in the Senate in accordance with other procedures of the Senate.

(7) A statement that information or a document is not published, or is confidential, or consists of advice to, or internal deliberations of, government, in the absence of specification of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document, is not a statement that meets the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4).

(8) If a minister concludes that a statement under paragraph (3) should more appropriately be made by the head of an agency, by reason of the independence of that agency from ministerial direction or control, the minister shall inform the committee of that conclusion and the reason for that conclusion, and shall refer the matter to the head of the agency, who shall then be required to provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (3).

(d) requires the Procedure Committee to review the operation of this order and report to the Senate by 20 August 2009.

(13 May 2009 J.1941)

CHAIR: The committee welcomes representatives from the Australian Securities and Investments Commission, and I particularly welcome Ms Sarah Court. As the incoming chair of the commission, this is her first estimates. We have your statement, which we can incorporate in the Hansard. Would you also like to speak to your opening statement?

Ms Court : Thank you, Chair. Good morning, everyone. I would, given it's my first time here as chair, if you would indulge me—just a few remarks. I do want to thank and acknowledge my predecessor, Joe Longo, for his stewardship of ASIC over the last five years.

We have done a range of important work in recent times, and I want to outline that in brief. We have strengthened our enforcement stance. We've taken decisive action against misconduct. We have obtained record penalties and record custodial sentences, while also advancing our key regulatory priorities. We've driven the landmark ASX inquiry. We have considerably contributed to thinking about public and private markets and made significant process with regulatory simplification, highlighting our role in helping to enhance productivity and support economic growth, and I am looking forward to building on this work in the coming years.

Given this is a budget estimates hearing, I want to give a brief update on a range of matters, including some initiatives funded in last month's federal budget. Firstly, the government is investing to complete tranche 2 of the RegistryConnect program to stabilise and uplift our business registers. This is very important work. It builds on previous funding and will help us improve online services for company registrations and lodgements. It will help us link director IDs to company records and upgrade registry systems. These registers are important because they support millions of everyday decisions, including extending credit, company verification, entering commercial arrangements and assessing risk.

The government is also investing to strengthen the oversight of managed investment schemes, and that measure will help improve ASIC's digital capability and help our tools access existing non-ASIC government data and enhance our supervision of that section. While we feel there is no silver bullet to the complex issues around managed investment schemes, having better access to data will help us respond to existing and emerging threats, including those highlighted by the First Guardian and Shield matters.

Turning to those matters, we have continued our range of extensive work, with a view to continuing to return money to investors who have lost funds. We've run a significant communications campaign to make sure that people are alerted to these issues and to encourage AFCA notifications. We currently have 14 proceedings in the Federal Court against 26 defendants, relating to these issues, and this number includes the second action we've recently taken against Equity Trustees for allegedly failing to meet its trustee obligations. This is the fifth matter that ASIC have taken against a super trustee as part of our investigations, and it means that we have now commenced proceedings against every trustee that made these funds available on their platforms. That work to date has resulted in the return of more than $420 million to investors.

This committee is often interested in ASIC's criminal work. We've recently seen significant custodial sentences imposed in a range of matters, including the sentencing of Anthony Torre to six years in prison for fraud involving the misappropriation of superannuation funds, Remedy Housing officials sentenced to lengthy prison terms and Rodney Forrest sentenced to more than five years in prison for insider trading. That was the first outcome of our new specialist insider trading team, and that matter was investigated and finalised within 16 months of the offending.

Finally—I'm sure we'll be talking about this this morning—we have commenced an investigation into allegations about the conduct of several registered company auditors at KPMG that came to light after whistleblower claims were first aired in the parliament. Our focus is to determine whether the conduct sanctioned by KPMG may be a breach of the duties of a registered company auditor. With that opening, Chair, thank you for the indulgence. We're ready now to take your questions.

CHAIR: Thanks very much, Ms Court. I will go to Senator Bragg first up.

Senator BRAGG: Good morning, and congratulations on your appointment.

Ms Court : Thank you, Senator.

Senator BRAGG: I have a couple of lines of questioning. One is in relation to a case, and another is in relation to, effectively, a policy change from ASIC. I noticed you talked about some of the financial collapses in your opening. In terms of the First Guardian victims, they are partially covered if they invested through Equity—is that right? What about those that didn't?

Ms Court : Through Equity Trustees? Is that what you're referring to?

Senator BRAGG: I guess what I'm trying to get from you is sort of a snapshot. What did the investors invest through? Which conduits did they use? Who's covered in the various compensation commitments and other actions? Who's not yet been helped?

Ms Court : It's a very good question, and it's a complicated answer, so I'll give it as best I can, but feel free to interrupt me, Senator, if I'm not giving you—

Senator BRAGG: I wouldn't do that!

Ms Court : the information that you need. The Shield and First Guardian master funds were made available on the platforms of four trustees: the Macquarie trustee, the Netwealth trustee, the Diversa trustee, and, in relation to Equity Trustees, both of the funds were made available on it. Both First Guardian and Shield were made available in relation to that.

In terms of the work that ASIC has been doing to get money back for investors, we've taken two approaches. The first thing that we did—this probably was 12 to 18 months ago—was to try to freeze all of the assets that were available in the funds to make sure that as many as possible were available to be returned to investors.

Senator BRAGG: Across all four?

Ms Court : Across the two funds.

Senator BRAGG: The two master funds, yes.

Ms Court : In relation to the Shield Master Fund freezing actions, I can get you the precise figures, but my recollection is we froze about $230-odd million that was sitting in that fund before those funds were disbursed. In relation to the First Guardian Master Fund, there were no funds there or very few funds. The liquidator is still doing its work in relation to First Guardian.

Senator BRAGG: That's what happens when you have a big fraud.

Ms Court : Well, whether it's a fraud or not, we are continuing our investigations, but certainly that's the manner in which these two cases are being discussed. We then sued, as I said, all of the trustees. Our real concern here was that the people that lost money in the Shield and First Guardian investments had their mandatory superannuation contributions sitting in an APRA regulated fund. They were persuaded through lead generators and then advised by financial advisers to move those funds into what were high-risk and illiquid property schemes.

Senator BRAGG: Can I just check with you that all the people that invested into First Guardian went through one of those four conduits?

Ms Court : No.

Senator BRAGG: Or did some go directly? Do you understand my question?

Ms Court : The vast majority go through one of those conduits.

Senator BRAGG: So almost all of the investors went through Macquarie, Netwealth, Diversa or Equity.

Ms Court : Indeed, Senator. Just to be completely clear, there were some that invested through self-managed super funds, but that percentage was quite small.

Senator BRAGG: I understand. Really my question about this is: have you taken action against all four of those organisations?

Ms Court : Yes, we have.

Senator BRAGG: So if I'm an investor through one of those four conduits, I could expect that I could look at what ASIC's done and say to myself, 'Well, they've done as much as they could to recover my moneys but also to take action to ensure that the people who are behind these things are facing serious repercussions.'

Ms Court : Yes. Well, again, without wanting to delve too much into the detail, ASIC's action against Macquarie and Netwealth has resulted in full returns of the capital to all of those investors—$420 million.

Senator BRAGG: That's Macquarie and that's—

Ms Court : Netwealth.

Senator BRAGG: What about Diversa and Equity?

Ms Court : Diversa and Equity have not made compensation or remediation available. We are—

Senator BRAGG: Because they have not accepted, necessarily, all the facts—is that right?

Ms Court : You'll have to ask them their reasons, but we are in court in relation to two actions against Equity Trustees and one action against Diversa, all of which are seeking compensation for those that were impacted by what we say were failures in their trustee obligations.

Senator BRAGG: What about the people who are running these schemes? First Guardian was a registered scheme, wasn't it?

Ms Court : Yes, it was.

Senator BRAGG: Who was the trustee for that? Sorry, it was a wholesale scheme.

Ms Court : It was a registered managed investment scheme.

Senator BRAGG: Who was the trustee or RE?

Ms Court : Falcon Capital.

Senator BRAGG: Did they provide RE services to others?

Ms Court : No, I don't believe so, but that's getting a bit more into the detail than I've got. I've got it in front of me somewhere.

Senator BRAGG: I just want to ask a simple question. Have you taken action against the directors on the RE of Falcon and everything else?

Ms Court : We are continuing investigations in relation to the people that sat behind, in our view, both of those failed funds—both the Shield Master Fund and the First Guardian Master Fund—and those investigations are continuing.

Senator BRAGG: You're still investigating?

Ms Court : Yes, we are.

Senator BRAGG: How long has the investigation gone for?

Ms Court : It's a good question. Given the breadth of these matters, our first focus was on protecting investor funds and taking freezing actions not just in relation to the funds themselves but in relation to a large number of—we have taken action in relation, for example, to all of the individuals we considered involved in the collapses, to freeze their funds and restrain their assets. That's been active. I think I said in my opening we've got 14 separate Federal Court proceedings against 26 individuals across the board, and that includes those involved in the funds, the trustees, financial advice firms, the ratings house and the like. We have been extraordinarily active on this, and we are now bringing to an end our investigations in relation to those individuals.

Senator BRAGG: You'd hope so. I think it's very important that ASIC can demonstrate that it can move quickly, particularly when you've been investigating for a long time these Falcon and First Guardian organisations, and that you can make the actions that are available to you under the Corporations Act as soon as possible. There is a sense—it's my opinion, for what it's worth—that sometimes it can take too long.

Ms Court : I appreciate you have that view, and I know we've talked about that previously. I do, though, think it's fair to push back on it slightly. We've taken a more interventionist and aggressive stance on these collapses than I think we've done in any other matter. We've stood up around 50 or 60 people who are working almost around the clock on these issues. Investigations of this nature that involve the dispersion of funds and moneys, both internationally and to various places domestically, do take time. As I said, our first priority here was to make sure that we recovered money for investors. While I appreciate investors will very much want to see people behind this held to account, we were conscious about making sure that we returned money to them, and we have made progress in that. We'd like to do more. We would absolutely like to do more.

Senator BRAGG: I understand that.

CHAIR: You're at eight minutes, Senator Bragg.

Senator BRAGG: I understand that, but you started the investigation into First Guardian in early 2024, so it's been more than two years. I hope you can move quickly. In relation to the Lion Property matter, I think you've had some engagement from the people who have lost significant funds. My understanding is—you'll correct me here if I'm wrong—effectively Lion was holding itself out to be some sort of licensed business. I don't think it was licensed. Is that right?

Ms Court : Yes, we have had extensive engagement; you're quite right.

Senator BRAGG: Is that right? It was holding itself out to be a business that was licensed in some form, as some sort of investment business, but it didn't have a licence, did it?

Ms Court : No, and I don't know that it's right to say that it was holding itself out to be licensed. For example, it didn't make representations, as I understand it, on its website to say, 'We're licensed,' when it wasn't. As you said, Lion never held an Australian financial services licence. As I understand it, its marketing was conducted predominantly through social media, mainly Facebook, and the people that invested money in Lion largely went through that. So there was no financial licence, there was no lead generation, and there were no financial advisers involved, as I understand it, in the Lion property.

Senator BRAGG: I guess one of the issues is this: that may be your very well-informed position, but I don't think that's the position of hundreds of people who invested in this thinking it was a licensed investment company, to use plain language. They thought that they were investing in an organisation or through an organisation where there would be some protections for their money. As we've discussed many times before, in a country like Australia, if people invest in an organisation that looks like it's licensed, then they would expect that the normal rules would apply if things go wrong, in cases like this, where fraud is alleged to have been undertaken. So the claim against ASIC from a large number of the Lion property investors has been one of defective administration. I understand that ASIC itself cannot issue any orders or instruments under the defective administration arrangements, but, if ASIC does undertake defective administration—if it does—it can be covered by the CDDA, can't it?

Ms Court : There are a lot of different topics that you're putting into that question, with respect—

Senator BRAGG: There may be.

Ms Court : If you want me to speak about the Lion issue in particular, I would just put on the record that, yes, we are very aware that there are a number of Lion investors who are very concerned about their loss of money.

Senator BRAGG: There are 600.

Ms Court : Yes, there's a significant number. So we are very aware of that. Indeed, as you've outlined, I think, in your question, one of the challenges for ASIC in a matter like Lion is that there was no financial services licence and there were no licence or registered providers involved at all. For people that invest, unfortunately, while I very much understand that they may think there are protections there, without a licence, there are many, many investment schemes that operate outside of the regulated system. I think one of the challenges for ASIC and one of the things that we're thinking about—and I'm not for a moment suggesting that this will help the Lion investors, which I very much acknowledge—is this: how do we help make sure people are very aware of where the regulated boundaries are and where the protections kick in and the importance of somebody that you hand your money to having an Australian financial services licence? That's what I'd say about Lion, and it's very different to the circumstances I was outlining in relation to Shield and First Guardian.

I will turn to the second part of your question, about the defective administration scheme. I will be corrected on this possibly by Mr Gregson if I get this wrong, but I believe that, yes, claims can be made against ASIC but they're not determined by ASIC, and I think you would expect that, because you wouldn't want us marking our own homework in that regard.

Senator BRAGG: That would be a conflict of interest. Finally, to clarify, it sounds like you're more open to being more aggressive in the future. We had Melissa Caddick carry on with a financial services business in Sydney for almost a decade. She was not licensed; she stole someone else's licence. You've got these poor people who think that they're swimming in-between the flags, so to speak. It's a big problem. We come to this bush capital, we make these laws, and we say, 'Here's what you've got to do to be a financial licensed business.' Then, over here, you've got all these crooks and shonks setting up fake businesses. Frankly, you've got to find a better way to close them down, because too many people are being hurt and then we've got to go through all of these different convoluted processes to try and help them. It chews up your resources, and, when people are going through the trouble of trying to apply for defective administration cases and the like, it's obviously very taxing for them. It would be much better if ASIC could give evidence in the future about how it's proposing to close down people who claim to be running a business that is licensed but who actually aren't.

Ms Court : I know we're at time, Chair, but, if I could just be given a minute or two to respond, Senator—

Senator BRAGG: Well, we'll be in trouble.

Ms Court : you've raised a very important point, I think. When you and I, and you and ASIC, have previously discussed these issues, I think you've come at that through the lens of enforcement and a concern ASIC's not taking aggressive enough enforcement. I've been reflecting a bit on that, and I think what we're really talking about here is not so much enforcement. We have an extraordinarily effective enforcement record, and I can talk to you about that at length. I won't, but I could.

I think what we're talking about is detection, early detection of where there are problems, and then what disruptive action—which is not necessarily traditional, court based enforcement. Do we issue stop orders? Do we put out public warnings? Do we put funds on an investor alert list? We talk about these issues within ASIC all of the time. We are deeply concerned that there are Australians that lose money to investment schemes and other opportunities all the time. We are very open to any suggestions or information about how we might do that better.

But this is a fine line, because many people make a lot of money and do very well out of these kinds of schemes and funds as well. We have to work out how quickly an agency like ASIC does intervene. Sometimes, when we intervene too early—and they're the matters you don't hear complaints about—then investors are very concerned with the action that we've taken, because they feel that we have shut down an investment opportunity that they were very happy with.

I'm not defensive at all; I think the points that you make are valid. I know you've been making them for a long time, and I'd just assure you that we are working hard to bring our data together, bring our intelligence together and, yes, take perhaps a more interventionist approach to shut things down at an early stage. I just want to be open that I do have a slight concern that you'll then start hearing concerns about ASIC being too activist in closing down things that people don't want us to. So we're in the middle of a rock and a hard place sometimes, but we are very much working on it and deeply concerned about the impact of failures like that of the Lion Property Group on investors.

CHAIR: Thank you. Senator McKim.

Senator McKIM: Good morning, folks. I've got some questions relating to the financial reporting of fossil fuel companies of their decommissioning and site restoration costs. I note that this area has been identified by ASIC as a focus area for your work in 2026-27. You're in receipt of a complaint from the Wilderness Society via its solicitors, who have raised concerns with you that Beach Energy and Amplitude Energy may have understated their decommissioning liabilities in their 2025 financial reports by making the assumption that offshore pipelines will be allowed to remain in situ despite a very clear legal obligation under the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Act and a regulatory presumption that full removal of infrastructure is the base-case expectation. I can say to you that I'm also aware you're in receipt of a complaint from somebody else in relation to Santos. I'm also aware that this is a widespread practice amongst fossil fuel companies. People like Woodside are making the same assumption in their financial reports. So can I, firstly, ask you: what action, if any, have you taken in response to the Wilderness Society's complaint?

Ms Court : Good morning. I'm going to pass you over to Commissioner O'Rourke on these issues.

Ms O'Rourke : Just to step back, before we come into the particular cases, you're right to say that ASIC has this as an area of focus. We do, each year, set out, in relation to financial reporting and audits, some areas of particular focus for us. When we did that in May, we did note that we'd review the disclosure of companies that have provisions for decommissioning and site restoration costs. This is subject to the Australian accounting standard AASB 137, which governs the provisioning of those costs. We have identified that because we think it is an important area of these financial reports and can prove it has had some difficulties or inconsistencies in the past. I can describe some work that we've taken in relation to Woodside in the past, but I'm going to have to take on notice your particular question on the Wilderness Society request.

Senator McKIM: I'm aware of what you've done in the past on Woodside, and I'm aware that they actually had to adjust their balance sheets significantly—basically because they were caught out lying. Those are my words, not yours.

Ms O'Rourke : Thank you.

Senator McKIM: But we did give you advance notice that we were going to raise this issue and I'm disappointed that you can't tell us now what you've done in relation to this. The Wilderness Society complaint went in in December last year, or perhaps in November. It was late last year. Can I just be clear—

Ms O'Rourke : Yes. I'm sorry; I understood that you'd have questions, but I hadn't appreciated that they would be on the specific inquiries or complaints. If, through the course of the morning, I can get that for you, I will, and I'll bring to that to your attention.

Senator McKIM: I'd appreciate that, thanks. At its heart, there is a widespread deliberate deception of the market happening across fossil fuel companies—including Beach, Amplitude, Santos and Woodside. Of course they're doing it because it makes their balance sheets look more positive than what they are in reality. This is a deliberate deception that creates significant investor risk, because the information that investors are relying on is not accurate. I want to take you through the argument here and ask you for a response.

In order to do that, I'll just go to Amplitude as an example. Amplitude stated in their 2025 annual report:

… offshore pipelines that are constructed from steel and concrete are assumed to remain in-situ, where it can be demonstrated that this will result in a net environmental benefit compared to full removal and where regulatory approval is anticipated to be obtained.

Subsequently that same annual report, for 2025, said:

Offshore pipelines that are constructed from steel and concrete have previously been accepted by the Australian regulator to be decommissioned in-situ, where it has been demonstrated that this will result in a net environmental benefit, compared to full removal.

My colleague Senator Whish-Wilson asked NOPSEMA about this in the 2025-26 additional estimates. Senator Whish-Wilson went through some context-setting, including raising the complaint to you from the Wilderness Society, and he asked NOPSEMA a very simple question: has NOPSEMA accepted any environment plans that would allow the in-situ abandonment of pipelines? NOPSEMA answered very clearly: no—no, they had not accepted any environment plans that allowed for the in-situ abandonment of pipelines. So when Amplitude informs its investors:

Offshore pipelines that are constructed from steel and concrete have previously been accepted by the Australian regulator to be decommissioned in-situ …

they are lying to their investors. NOPSEMA have put the lie to Amplitude's claim. Does that concern you?

Ms O'Rourke : Thank you for bringing the particulars of that complaint to our attention in this setting. Like I said, I'll have a closer look outside this hearing to see if we can provide anything in addition t that. I can just reiterate ASIC's interest in this as an area of important disclosure. That's why we've chosen it as one of our areas of focus. It is important that people understand the costs—as you pointed out, they can be very significant if there does actually have to be decommissioning and removal. I know you said you're familiar with it, but I'll just note that, after inquiries from ASIC, Woodside Energy did provide an additional $239 million for restoration costs in 2022.

Senator McKIM: Yes, because they got caught out of line.

Ms O'Rourke : So there is a lot of expense at stake here.

Senator McKIM: There is.

Ms O'Rourke : I'd acknowledge that and that it's an area of focus for ASIC.

Senator McKIM: Thank you. But it's also an area of significant potential risk for investors, is it not?

Ms O'Rourke : The importance of disclosure is for investors and for the integrity of the market.

Senator McKIM: And Woodside had to readjust its balance sheet significantly in response to previous work that ASIC did. Given the widespread assumptions that are used by fossil fuel companies to underpin their financial reporting—here, the assumption that some infrastructure will be allowed to remain in situ—then it's fair to say that that would constitute a potentially significant financial risk for investors, would it not?

Ms O'Rourke : You can see that we've had this area of focus in the past, noting the Woodside outcome that we've just discussed. We've just announced it as an area of focus for our upcoming financial year. We will be looking carefully at this issue. I agree that part of the reason, and the impact of that, will be for investors and for the companies.

Senator McKIM: You've said you'll be looking at this issue. Will you, when looking at this issue, include a consideration of whether the assumptions that are underpinning those provisions that are widely used in the fossil fuel industry—and those assumptions, again, are that some infrastructure will be allowed to remain in situ. We received information from KPMG on 29 April, which alerted us to the fact that there were some individuals that were being investigated by KPMG, including three registered company auditors that it was proposing to sanction. There was a flurry of activity—as, no doubt, the senators will recall—last Friday, when the then CEO and head of audit resigned. Since that time, we have commenced our formal investigation, earlier this week, and I should also make clear that we have issued multiple compulsory notices throughout that period to KPMG, and the formal investigation is underway.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: You mentioned three auditors specifically. Is that the total sum of individuals you're currently investigating, or—

Ms Court : Yes. I think it's fair to say that there are three registered company auditors that are currently within the scope of what we were looking at. But I have to say that this is an ever-moving feast at the moment, as more information comes our way, so I don't know that that will be the end of it.

I should also say, just to be helpful, that we've talked in this committee previously about some of the limits on ASIC's jurisdictional reach in relation to partnerships, and, of course, KPMG is a partnership. So we are thinking internally at ASIC about what our various regulatory hooks may be, in relation to the conduct that is being revealed. Needless to say, we have deep concerns about what has been revealed in the press, and we are trying to get to the bottom of the evidence as to those various incidents.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: I want to come to the hooks that you have available to you in a moment. Does ASIC know exactly why Andrew Yates resigned as CEO?

Ms Court : I don't have that information with me, no.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: What powers do you have to take action against any KPMG partners involved in this scandal? I'm recollecting the previous chair's statements about the capacity of ASIC to regulate—'just a sliver' were his words. Are we still in that regulatory no-man's-land? Can you reflect on the levers that are available to you and how you intend to exercise them?

Ms Court : Yes. As I said, our jurisdiction is available only in relation to some individuals that sit within a partnership, and those are people that are registered company auditors, those senior auditors that sign off on accounts. They have various professional obligations, and that is our most clear regulatory hook. There may be some other regulatory hooks in the sense that partnerships often have a range of proprietary companies that also sit within them, like service companies, for example. So there may be an option for ASIC to give that some consideration: were any of the directors that were sitting in relation to those proprietary companies within the partnership, and does that give us any broader opportunity? I should also note, of course, just for completeness, that there are regulators of partnerships, but they are the state based regulators.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: They are utterly inadequate to the project of regulating these behemoths, and what you're describing is an incredibly complex structure—

Ms Court : It is.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: that you have to find your way through to try and find a hook to regulate a multibillion-dollar operation. These are very large partnerships. Can you refer these partners to the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions for criminal prosecution?

Ms Court : I might have to take that on notice. I would have to take on notice whether or not the potential contraventions that relate to registered company auditors are criminal offences. I suspect they're not, but I can take that on notice for you, Senator.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: Thank you. Has ASIC determined if any of these KPMG staff responsible for the scandal are Australian financial services licence authorised representatives—AFSL?

Ms Court : We do know that there are AFSL holders—that some of the companies that I referred to a moment ago do hold an AFSL. But I just want to emphasise that we are really at the very early stages of looking at things that are, as I say, evolving as we speak.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: But your powers essentially relate to the pursuit of individuals—auditors. The problem here is a systemic, very large entity which you do not have powers to regulate or pursue. Am I right in saying that? I see you nodding.

Ms Court : Yes, you are, Senator, as we've discussed before. We think there is a regulatory gap in relation to the ability for ASIC—or any regulator, for that matter—to oversee what are enormous partnerships. Yes, our regulatory hook, for want of a better word is, as you outline, in relation to those individuals that are registered company auditors.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: I want to come to your own relationship with KPMG. I understand that ASIC has at least nine active contracts with KPMG. Have I got that right? Is that about the right number, and are they at the value of about $3 million?

Ms Court : It sounds like you are very well informed, Senator Pocock, but I'm going to pass to the CEO, Scott Gregson, who has that information.

Mr Gregson : The information I have is that we currently have eight active contracts. Six of those are for services contracts and two for consultancy contracts. Yes, the total of those is approximately $3 million.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: Does KPMG play any role in audit, internal or otherwise, within KPMG? I know historically they have. Can you give me the historic and the current picture on KPMG's involvement in internal audit, or any element of audit?

Mr Gregson : In relation to ASIC's dealings?

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: Yes.

Mr Gregson : I can advise that, of those contracts, none involve the company audit areas of KPMG that are in question. Of the eight current contracts, none relate to our audit function.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: I have details of those. I'm going to come to them. How are you managing your active contracts with KPMG given your investigation of them?

Mr Gregson : We continue to manage contracts in accordance with our normal practices and procedures. In light of these matters and in engaging with the Department of Finance, who are managing a whole-of-government response, we've also approached KPMG this week. We're seeking assurances of the absence of involvement of those persons involved in the matters that are public. We are also seeking assurances that their obligations as to confidentiality and treatment of secure information remain intact. We've had an interim response giving us that confirmation, and we're continuing to work with KPMG on those fronts.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: Have you sought assurances about the security of all your information, and have KPMG assured you that all of ASIC's information is secure?

Mr Gregson : That's right. We've sought that confirmation, we've had an interim response giving us that, we're continuing—

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: What does interim mean?

Mr Gregson : It means that we expect a further, more detailed response next week, but the initial response gives us that confirmation.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: Two of your current contracts commenced after ASIC commenced these inquiries and after a meeting with KPMG on 14 April, which the chair mentioned. One is a $249,000 contract for digital financial advice commenced on 18 May, and the other is a contract for strategic planning consultation services commenced on 4 May. That's a two-month contract where KPMG—at least on the surface—are advising ASIC on strategy. What do you say about that contract and the commencement of these two contracts after you'd become aware of the very serious allegations in relation to KPMG? Why have you commenced them, and what is this business of strategic advice from KPMG as you are investigating them?

Mr Gregson : We, obviously, follow appropriate procurement practices, and they are operated independently of many of our other activities in the agency. That's appropriate under the procurement rules. In relation to the two matters you referred to, your information is correct. That's publicly published. The 4 May contract in relation to support is fairly small. It's to help us establish some of our program management office needs in a particular IT project.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: Program office needs—what does that mean?

Mr Gregson : We operate a number of programs. This one relates to RegistryConnect, which provides enhancements to our registry operations. It's a large digital program. Within that program, you need program management office services. The services here help us with the expertise to set up that system.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: What's your protocol in relation to contracting with people you have under investigation or hold serious concerns about, simultaneously with those concerns and indeed with live investigations?

Mr Gregson : It's appropriate, for the most part, that we manage procurement independently of our investigations and actions.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: So you have no problem doing business with people you're investigating? You have no procedure?

Mr Gregson : Indeed, it's appropriate that we do have separation of some of that information.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: I don't think that passes any kind of pub test, frankly. That is a real concern. Will you continue with these contracts? Will you consider following the example of the RBA, the ATO and many others, including Lendlease, who is changing its audit and going out to market after many years of working with KPMG? Will you review these contracts, and will you review your relationship with KPMG?

Mr Gregson : The interest in approaching KPMG is to get information about how they're treating our information and how they're going to respond to those issues. Once we receive that, absolutely, we'll consider where we are with KPMG with respect to those current matters and the extent to which it should be relevant for our future procurement activities.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: Great. I'll come back.

Senator ROBERTS: Thank you, Chair, and thank you all for being here. Ms Roxanne Mysko is a whistleblower who has not been protected by whistleblower legislation as she should have been. Ms Mysko followed whistleblower protocol to the letter and has been on the receiving end of significant retribution for her disclosures as a whistleblower. Evidence shows ECS was contracted to Santos, Ensign Energy and Easternwell. Why has ASIC shown zero statutory duty to uphold the whistleblower safety act and laws? Ms Court : Thank you, Senator Roberts, and good morning. I know you have raised this issue with us previously, so thank you for your question. Senator ROBERTS: Could we have a private briefing?

Ms Court : Of course, Senator, we'd be very happy to give you a briefing. I am aware that the issues you've raised date back, I think, to 2022, as you said in your question. Ms Court : Thank you Senator, that's good of you. We will take you up on that.

Senator ROBERTS: I'll ask some more questions, but just tell me if they're appropriate or not. Why has ASIC not protected Ms Roxanne Mysko since the amended whistleblower act commenced on 1 January 2020?

Ms Court : I can answer one part of that question, if that would be of assistance? We take whistleblowing complaints very seriously. CHAIR: Senator Nampijinpa Price.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: You've pointed to insolvency rates as a proportion of registered companies. In absolute terms, however, almost 15,000 businesses entered external administration in the 2025 financial year. Does ASIC accept that policymakers should consider both the insolvency rate and the absolute number of business failures?

Ms O'Rourke : I think that both are relevant figures.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Does ASIC consider the absolute number of business failures to be economically significant, regardless of the insolvency rate?

Ms O'Rourke : That's a challenging question, because I'm not sure what you mean by 'economically significant'. I've acknowledged that they're both important. From our perspective, we measure insolvency numbers and share the data. Like I explained earlier, we assess and administer the frameworks associated with insolvency, whether they be for small businesses, large businesses or both. I'd also draw your attention to the Productivity Commission review that has just been launched which looks at business dynamism more generally and which also has the effectiveness of Australia's insolvency and bankruptcy frameworks as one of its specific areas of focus. In particular, it looks at one reform, regarding phoenixing: it's called 'creditor-defeating disposition'. That's one of those frameworks that I referred to which we administer. There's an active level of interest in the frameworks and, certainly in ASIC, a team and an area that administers the frameworks that we have.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Okay. Construction remains the largest source of insolvencies, and accommodation and food the second largest. Does ASIC have any evidence that conditions are improving materially in either sector?

Ms O'Rourke : The data that we collect in relation to insolvency is predominantly backward-looking: current- or former-state rather than prospective. I think your question goes to whether there are improvements in those sectors, and I don't think that we have data—at least that we've published—that's relevant to that.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Would it be fair to say that both sectors remain under significant pressure?

Ms O'Rourke : It's fair to say that the data we've shared shows that those are the biggest two that we've seen in relation to insolvencies. Yes, that's our current data.

Ms Court : It might just be worth noting—and correct me if I'm wrong, Commissioner O'Rourke—that ASIC's role in relation to the insolvency figures is really that we are collecting data. We are getting all of the information that comes in from the sector. We are trying to make sure that there are efficient ways for businesses throughout the economy, whether they be small or large, to have external administrators appointed.

Particularly in relation to small business, which your questions have been about, there is a particular process called a small-business restructure, which was introduced to specifically try to make it easier for small businesses when they reach these kinds of insolvency scenarios. One of the things we've been trying to do is to make that process more streamlined and easier for those involved, and we've seen some uplift in those figures. Generally, in terms of our work here, we're getting all that data in. We're trying to make it publicly available for people to see what the trends are and the reasons businesses are giving, but we're not necessarily the agency that's providing commentary or views on why it's happening or what we should do about it, if that helps.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Sitting in my position, I can make clear that, from the evidence you've provided, there are probably some concerns around that.

Ms Court : There are certainly high raw numbers of insolvencies. As you say, the key areas impacted in our statistics are construction, accommodation and hospitality—that's absolutely right—but there are more and more. I think the point Commissioner O'Rourke was making is that there are more and more companies out there. To some extent it makes sense that the numbers get higher.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: More than three-quarters of recent insolvencies involve small business. Does ASIC accept that insolvency statistics only capture businesses that ultimately fail and not the much larger number experiencing financial distress?

Ms O'Rourke : Our data doesn't systematically capture companies in financial distress. There are some aspects that we see. For example, with the small-business restructuring process that I described before, we get information about companies who successfully use that process. Like I explained before, that actually results in a company continuing to trade. It compromises with its creditors and then has new life after that. We do see some segments of companies that don't actually end up being wound up or enter insolvency or liquidation, but it's partial. I think you're alluding to there being a much larger group of companies that might have some level of financial strain, and our ASIC data doesn't comprehensively capture that.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: It doesn't comprehensively capture that.

Ms O'Rourke : It does not.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Does ASIC consider that there is value in policymakers understanding broader indicators of financial distress, rather than focusing solely on formal insolvencies?

Ms O'Rourke : I think that would be a question better posed to those policymakers. Indeed, I think it will be considered by the Productivity Commission, which is undertaking that wider look at business dynamism, including insolvency.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: When did ASIC first identify that insolvencies were accelerating?

Ms O'Rourke : ASIC has been tracking and publishing the data for quite a long period of time and sharing that information with people who can then draw their own insights about sectors or about the size of companies. I don't think we have a specific answer to your question. Sorry, I can specifically find out when we started publishing the data. I know it's been for a very long period of time, but, as our chair explained, we don't publish insights—

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: From 2022 to now, I suppose.

Ms O'Rourke : We don't draw and publish economic insights. We share some of the data. From that, you can see things like sectors and aspects of it. Like our chair explained earlier, we do have some fields about some of those causes—cash flow or trading losses and things like that—that we try and share. Our goal has been to increase the visibility and capacity for people to interrogate the data that we share so that they can draw their own insights.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: What warning indicators have been observed?

Ms O'Rourke : I'm sorry, would you mind explaining? Do you mean to ASIC or to businesses or to whom?

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: In relation to businesses and the increase in insolvencies.

Ms O'Rourke : I'm not sure I can assist you with that. I'm sorry, Senator.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: You mentioned phoenix activity. What proportion of insolvencies involve phoenix activity?

Ms O'Rourke : That's a very difficult question to answer. We, of course, along with the ATO and others are very concerned about illegal phoenixing activity. We do administer those creditor-defeating disposition provisions which are aimed to identify and respond in a regulatory sense to unlawful phoenixing. Part of that is that ASIC has a power by which certain dispositions of assets can be reversed because they've been identified as being a creditor-defeating disposition. I'll be able to get you information on how many times we've done that, but by no means would I describe that as a full set of all of those. They're the ones that we've been able to identify under those sorts of provisions. I think that concern around illegal phoenixing, like I said, has been longstanding. We work with the ATO and others as part of the illegal phoenixing taskforce to see if we can find other indicia and then act across the different agencies as appropriate.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: So you'll be able to provide that information on—

Ms O'Rourke : There'll be some additional information about the number of creditor-defeating disposition actions that ASIC has taken, and anything that I can help with from the phoenixing taskforce such as the number of phoenixing that's been identified. I think there have been some surveys; I'm not sure how dated they are, but we'll share that as available.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Would there be any opportunity to provide some of that activity by industry?

Ms O'Rourke : If available, of course. I'll see what we've got.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Can I ask just one last bunch to take on notice?

Ms Court : Senator, obviously we'll give you as much information on the phoenixing as we can. One complication is that 'phoenixing' is a very broad and wide term. There's no actual statutory definition of phoenixing. There are a range of statutory provisions in the Corporations Act but also, as Commissioner O'Rourke said, in many other pieces of legislation that all go to trying to prevent illegal phoenixing. We can absolutely give you as much information as we can, but it'll be pulling information from a range of different places, and it may well not cover the field because there are a range of other agencies involved in trying to combat illegal phoenixing.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: I've got some further questions that I can provide on notice.

CHAIR: I appreciate that, thank you. Senator Chandler.

Senator CHANDLER: I want to ask some questions about young Australians investing and the financial advice that they're receiving, and then I'll pivot to some questioning around the cost of financial advice. Since the budget, we've seen a lot of commentary and claims about the level that young Australians are investing at. I know some claims have said that nine in 10 people under 35 don't have any shares. I do note that ASIC's Moneysmart gen Z report in 2026 says that 23 per cent of young people invest in crypto, so that's almost a quarter, and that 18 per cent are investing in shares or ETFs, so around one in five. What is your understanding of the type of investments young Australians are currently engaging with?

Ms Court : I'm going to pass you to Commissioner Kirkland, who'll be able to answer that for you.

Mr Kirkland : We published some data on 16 March, which was survey based data. I'm conscious there is a range of data sources around. Some is based on transaction data. In this case it was survey data. It was based on a nationally representative online survey of 1,127 Australians aged 18 to 28 that was conducted in November and December last year. It found that 18 per cent of gen Z respondents reported that they owned shares. If you can give me a moment, I'll be able to just get some of the information on some of the other asset classes, which I know I'll have available somewhere here. We did find that almost one in four also reported that they owned cryptocurrency, so that was 23 per cent.

Senator CHANDLER: In your survey, when asked about savings priorities, young people listed shares and crypto as No. 2 and No. 3 respectively, just behind a traditional savings account. With the rise of crypto and ETF trading by young Australians, how has ASIC had to adapt its monitoring roles and its information-providing roles according to that change of investor profile?

Mr Kirkland : I'll take the second part of that question first. In a way, the survey that we've just been talking about is part of the change in our approach. We've had the Moneysmart website for a long period of time and we know it's heavily used by Australians—visited by over 11 million users in the last calendar year, I believe. It's been a key source of information for all Australians in relation to financial decisions, but one of the key groups that we've decided to focus on assisting more is young Australians, particularly in relation to investments. In order to better help them, we have undertaken research to understand their behaviours and their aspirations. We have produced a lot of new content on Moneysmart that's specifically tailored to their needs, and we've also increased our social media activity, particularly in the form of posts and short video content on platforms like Instagram. And we're constantly experimenting with different ways to engage with young Australians and trying to improve how we get that information out.

In relation to our monitoring activity, the other key thing we've really focused on has been some behaviour of concern in relation to what we call 'finfluencers'—influencers on social media providing information on financial topics. That's not necessarily a concern, but, if people are operating in Australia and giving financial advice, then that's something that requires a license or an authorisation from a licensee. Over the last two years, we've undertaken two waves of action in relation to finfluencers that we consider to be potentially operating in breach of the law. That's been part of globally coordinated action with regulators in a number of jurisdictions, and it's involved issuing formal warning letters to a number of finfluencers. We've seen a number of changes in their practices as a result.

Senator CHANDLER: So this a clear and growing trend, from your perspective? This isn't just a small component of investment activity that we're talking about?

Mr Kirkland : We measure some of this behaviour sporadically, so it's not data that we're gathering on a quarterly or annual basis in a way that's intended to give a reliable indication of trends, but it is clear that many young Australians are, on the one hand, obtaining and seeking information about financial decisions online and, on the other hand, entertaining investments in newer asset classes, such as crypto related investments.

Senator CHANDLER: I note the Treasurer was asked about this gen Z ASIC report that we've been talking about in one of his postbudget interviews, when he was talking about young Australians and some of his claims were being queried. He said:

… it's—

ASIC—

an independent regulator—but, yes, understood … I'll check that out.

Has the Treasurer reached out to ASIC to become informed on the extent of young Australians investing since then?

Mr Kirkland : I'm not in a position to answer that—not that I'm aware of, but we can certainly take that on notice.

Senator CHANDLER: I think one of the questions here is whether young Australians are turning to finfluencers, AI to get their financial advice because they are locked out of affordable, traditional financial advice. Do you think that's a concern?

Mr Kirkland : In terms of the proposition, we haven't gathered evidence on the reasons that young people might be turning to some of these newer sources of information. I should also say that, in terms of the way that we framed the questions in some of that research on where younger people were going for financial information, it wasn't framed in terms of financial advice as defined under the law. We asked about sources that people use for financial information when making financial decisions, so it may have captured a broader range of needs and inquiries than what people might turn to a financial adviser for.

Senator CHANDLER: Going to some of those cost questions now—just to provide an example, first up, of the sorts of extra costs financial advisers face, in September 2025 advisers faced a CSLR based levy of $1,295 per adviser. In March 2026, advisers faced an ASIC funding levy of $2,398 per adviser. In May 2026, advisers faced a CSLR special levy of $665 per adviser plus a further $1,312 CSLR based levy for the next financial year. That's thousands of dollars per adviser before they've had to account for rent, wages, insurance, technology, education, CPD, all the things they have to do. Has ASIC modelled how these levies affect the cost of advice and access to advice, particularly for young Australians?

Mr Kirkland : To my knowledge, we have not. I should say, in relation to some of those regimes—for instance, in the Compensation Scheme of Last Resort, we have a really narrow and particular role in that we oversee the operations of the CSLR operator and we issue the invoices, but the broader CSLR regime is really a matter for government. That's one of the reasons we're not undertaking that sort of broader analysis on the various costs of heading into financial advice.

Senator CHANDLER: Have you undertaken any modelling to understand whether these levies are affecting the number of advisers leaving the profession—because it's just too expensive to stay in it?

Mr Kirkland : To my knowledge, we have not, although, in terms of numbers of advisers overall, it is something that we've taken an interest in. There have obviously been a range of reforms that have kicked in in recent times, including some of the educational qualification requirements and the requirement for those to be registered on our register. There was a lot of concern around whether that would result in any decline in the number of advisers, and I think it's probably fair to say that the number of advisers is holding relatively steady. As at 30 April 2026, it was 15,152, compared to 15,435 as at 30 June 2024.

Senator CHANDLER: With the increased compliance costs on advisers on the one hand and the increased number of Australians—young Australians in particular, as we've talked about this morning, but I suspect it's more general than that—seeking financial advice from other, less registered sources, whether it's finfluencers or using artificial intelligence to come up with their financial advice, do we have a concern that we might in effect end up doing what we did with illicit tobacco and making the act of pursuing the regulated route so expensive that we just end up pushing people into unregulated forms of getting that same advice?

Mr Kirkland : I think those questions in many ways are broader policy questions for government because the design of the overall regime relating to financial advice and issues such as the CSLR really are government matters. I think our role is to oversee those regimes: in relation to financial advisers, to oversee the licensing regime; to take targeted action in relation to the conduct of financial advisers; and, more broadly, to provide information to help assist Australians to make financial decisions in their best interests wherever they may be going for information to assist them in those decisions.

Senator CHANDLER: Are you comfortable with Australians getting financial advice from artificial intelligence or people on TikTok?

Because that's a significant amount. As we've heard today, the structure of business in Australia is made up of more than 90 per cent small businesses. If you look at small businesses, how many of those are actually trust structures? Do you have any idea about that?

Ms McAlary-Smith : We don't have that data.

Senator Gallagher: I think the data that Treasury provided is that 90 per cent of small businesses would not be affected by the reforms to trust arrangements, and there is, as part of the reforms, a three-year opportunity to restructure and reform without any cost.

Senator LIDDLE: I do get your point here, but we also know that most businesses in Australia are small businesses. How many we actually talking about?

Senator Gallagher: About 2.7 million.

Ms McAlary-Smith : It's 2.7, yes. It's around 97 per cent of businesses in Australia.

Senator LIDDLE: Where do we get an indication of how many of those would be structured in that way?

Senator Gallagher: It's so late, but I'm sure the figure is that around 90 per cent of small businesses would not be affected by the reforms to trusts.

Ms McAlary-Smith : The information I have from Treasury is that around 350,000 active small businesses operate through a discretionary trust structure, which accounts for around 15 per cent of all active small businesses. Senator LIDDLE: Thank you.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: ASBFEO has been named in the budget and by the small business minister as the group that will provide guidance to small businesses that have to restructure. Do you have a timeline for when that advice could be ready?

Ms McAlary-Smith : From January 2027.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Are you looking into how much it will cost these businesses to go through these restructures—accounting fees and state taxes like stamp duty?

Ms McAlary-Smith : We're working through and taking advice from advisers in terms of what their estimates of costs will actually be. We will await the passage through the parliament, and then we will regroup after that.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: ASBFEO has historically called for a more consistent definition of 'small business' at around a $10 million turnover to reduce regulatory complexity. Why was that preferred to $2 million?

Ms McAlary-Smith : With respect to the definition of 'small business', my particular view is that you're right; there're a multitude of definitions that are currently in use, and that's at all levels of government, across a variety of definitions. Invariably, small businesses can find themselves sometimes on the wrong side of a definition, irrespective of what that definition actually is. One of the challenges we have around harmonisation of a singular definition of 'small business' is that if there's a way to harmonise it so that no small business is worse off, then that would be fantastic, but that would be a significant challenge. In terms of what threshold and in what context, our advice and my view, as with the current ombudsman, is that, with respect to policy designers and decision-makers, it is best to focus on the issue at hand in terms of how we are trying to help small businesses, provide supports or perhaps provide some relief regulatory as well, rather than necessarily having a fully aligned definition across all definitions.

Ideally, certainly within a singular piece of legislation, you would like to see the definition be the same, and certainly there could be opportunities to be a bit more principles based, for example. If it's revenue, what is the revenue that we're looking at? If it's employee number, is it FTE, or is it headcount? What potentially is a range of that as well? In our experience, the actual question at hand is a big feeder into what might be that appropriate definition.
